planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes; as one of the original Superbena colors, Blue is sold only as a vegetatively propagated transplant, never from seed, and settles in fastest when planted while nights are still cool.

directions: Superbena Blue was among the first colors released in the original Superbena line and remains a garden standard for a true, clear violet-blue trailing verbena that holds its color without fading in strong summer sun. The vigorous, mildew-resistant habit spills 18 to 30 inches over a container edge or knits together as a fast groundcover in a sunny bed, flowering continuously from planting until frost without any deadheading. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water around the crown is the most common cause of decline in trailing verbena. Its cool blue tone is a natural foil for warm-colored companions like orange lantana or yellow bidens in mixed plantings.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Blue Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes into well-drained soil; Coral is a warm-toned original Superbena color that combines well with tropical-style container plantings.

directions: Coral carries clusters of soft salmon-orange flowers with a faint peachy blush, a warmer and gentler tone than the saturated reds and burgundies elsewhere in the Superbena line. Like its series-mates it was bred for strong resistance to the powdery mildew that plagues older trailing verbena through humid Gulf Coast summers, and it flowers non-stop from spring through the first hard frost without deadheading. The trailing, mounding habit works equally well cascading from a raised planter or filling in as a sunny groundcover between shrubs. Pair it with blue salvia or silver-leaved dusty miller for a soft, warm-and-cool container combination.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Coral Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes; Large Purple was one of the founding colors of the Superbena line and remains a benchmark for flower size within the series.

directions: Large Purple earns its name from flower heads noticeably bigger than typical trailing verbena, packed with rich violet-purple blooms on vigorous, fast-spreading stems. It shares the whole Superbena series' hallmark resistance to powdery mildew and its ability to keep flowering through summer heat without deadheading, traits that set the line apart from older seed-grown trailing verbena when it was introduced. Use it to fill large hanging baskets and window boxes quickly, since a single plant can cascade two feet or more by midsummer. Cut plants back by a third if they become sparse in the center after a heavy flowering flush to encourage fresh growth.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Large Purple Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes into well-drained soil; Peach carries a soft, muted tone that reads best in morning or late-day light.

directions: Peach bears soft apricot-peach flowers with a subtle pink undertone, a muted pastel that softens the bright jewel tones common elsewhere in the Superbena line. The trailing habit and non-stop bloom from spring to frost are consistent with the rest of the series, as is its resistance to the powdery mildew that shortens the season for many older trailing verbena selections. Its gentle color works particularly well in cottage-style mixed containers alongside dusty miller, heliotrope, or soft yellow bidens. Provide full sun and sharp drainage, since waterlogged soil is the most common cause of stem rot in trailing verbena.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Peach Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes into well-drained, fertile soil; Wine's deep tone reads darkest in cooler spring and fall temperatures.

directions: Wine produces dense clusters of deep maroon-red flowers, a darker and more purple-shaded tone than the brighter burgundy elsewhere in the Superbena line, giving container plantings a moody, richly saturated accent. Growth habit, bloom continuity, and mildew resistance match the rest of the series, and the plant flowers without a break from spring planting through the first hard freeze. Its dark coloring is especially effective paired with chartreuse foliage or white-flowered companions that make the deep tone pop rather than recede. Shear lightly if stems become leggy by midsummer to keep the mound dense and full of color.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Wine Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes into well-drained soil; Whiteout is prized for its especially large, dense flower umbels among white-flowered trailing verbena.

directions: Whiteout produces unusually large, dense umbels of pure white flowers that trial reports have long used as a benchmark for flower size within the Superbena line. The clean white color brightens shaded corners of a container arrangement and pairs neutrally with almost any other color in the series, making it a common anchor plant in mixed hanging baskets. It shares the series-wide resistance to powdery mildew and continuous bloom habit, flowering without deadheading from spring planting to the first hard frost. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, since white-flowered verbena selections show soil-borne leaf spot diseases more readily against their pale petals than darker colors do.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Whiteout Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last hard frost danger passes into well-drained soil; Royale Sangria is part of the upgraded Royale line bred for even larger flowers and denser coverage than the original Superbena series.

directions: Royale Sangria bears rich wine-red flowers with a darker central eye, giving each umbel more visual depth than the flatter color of older Superbena reds. The Royale line was bred from the original Superbena series for even larger flower clusters, tighter branching, and denser overall coverage, and Sangria's saturated color makes it a strong focal plant rather than just a filler in mixed containers. It flowers continuously from spring through the first hard frost without deadheading and holds up to Gulf South heat and humidity far better than older seed-grown trailing verbena. Full sun and sharp drainage keep the dense, mounding habit free of the powdery mildew that shortens the season for less resistant selections.
sources: Proven Winners - Superbena Royale Sangria Verbena Grower Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Trailing Verbena for Florida Containers

common_name: Greystone Daphne Verbena (Rose-Pink Clumping Groundcover Verbena)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plugs in spring into well-drained garden soil in full sun; Greystone Daphne is a much older selection than the newer Homestead series but shares the same reliable cold hardiness of straight Verbena canadensis.

directions: Greystone Daphne is a long-grown selection of the native Southeastern species prized for its large, rounded heads of clear rose-pink flowers held above finely cut, dark green foliage. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense mat that tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than bedding-type hybrid verbena, making it a dependable perennial groundcover along a sunny bank or border edge. Unlike tender trailing verbena hybrids, it dies back to a hardy crown in cold winters and returns reliably each spring across a wide hardiness range. Shear the mat back hard in late winter or after the first flush of bloom to renew dense growth and encourage a strong rebloom into fall.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Verbena canadensis
Norman Winter - Southern horticultural trade press

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall onto disturbed, compacted, or poor soil in full sun; bracted vervain germinates readily in the exact rough conditions — gravel edges, trampled paths, dry waste ground — that discourage most garden annuals.

directions: Bracted vervain is a low, sprawling native wildflower found across nearly all of North America on compacted, disturbed, and gravelly ground where few other flowering plants persist, its small lavender-blue flowers nearly hidden among conspicuous leafy bracts along each stem. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and needs no supplemental irrigation or fertilizer, thriving instead on neglect in lean or heavy clay soil that would stunt most bedding plants. Use it deliberately as a tough, low groundcover for gravel paths, parking strip edges, or other hot, compacted sites rather than a refined border, since its sprawling habit and modest flowers favor function over show. It self-sows readily and can be mowed or trimmed back hard without harm if it spreads further than wanted.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or plugs after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Peruvian verbena is one of the parent species behind many modern red-flowered trailing verbena hybrids and shares their need for sharp drainage.

directions: Peruvian verbena is a mat-forming South American species covered through the warm season in small, intensely scarlet-red flower clusters held just above finely divided, semi-evergreen foliage. It hugs the ground more tightly than most trailing hybrid verbena, rooting along its trailing stems as it spreads, which makes it useful as a fast-covering groundcover on a sunny bank or spilling over a low retaining wall. Once established it tolerates considerable heat and drought on lean, gravelly, or sandy soil, but resents heavy clay and poor drainage, especially through humid summers. It behaves as a woody-based perennial in mild winter climates and can be cut back hard in late winter to keep growth dense and floriferous.
sources: Pacific Bulb Society / Southwest native plant references

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or plugs after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; moss verbena has naturalized across much of the warm Southern and Southwestern US and self-sows readily once established.

directions: Moss verbena forms a dense, ferny mat of finely dissected foliage smothered in small lavender-purple flower clusters through the warm season, low enough to use between stepping stones or cascading over a sunny rock wall. It is markedly drought tolerant once rooted in, thriving on lean, gravelly, or sandy soil with little supplemental water, and it dislikes rich, consistently moist ground where it tends to rot. The plant has naturalized widely in the warm Southern US, reseeding freely in gravel drives and disturbed roadside soil, so gardeners in its naturalized range should expect volunteer seedlings each spring. Shear the mat back by half after the first flush of bloom to keep growth tight and encourage a second wave of flowers into fall.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring into average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Rocky Mountain and Southwestern native tolerates cold winters far better than most garden verbena.

directions: Spike verbena is an upright native of Southwestern and Rocky Mountain mountain meadows, sending up stiff, square stems topped with dense, elongated spikes of small reddish-purple flowers that open gradually from the base upward over a long summer season. Unlike the low, trailing verbena grown in most garden beds, it stands tall and stiffly upright, making it useful as a vertical accent in a native or xeric perennial border rather than as a groundcover. It thrives in lean, well-drained, even rocky soil with minimal supplemental water once established, and excess fertility or moisture tends to produce floppy, weak stems. The tubular flowers are a strong late-summer draw for native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds at higher elevations and in cold-winter climates where many other verbena are not reliably hardy.
